title: F3 – External analysis I: PESTEL and Porter's Five Forces
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 3 „External analysis“ (Teil 1) und der Five-Forces-Analyse im Dyson-Fall

blocks.text: Layers of the business environment: macro-environment (PESTEL) → industry (Five Forces) → competitors and strategic groups → the organization.

Industry explains a large share of firm performance – hence the interest in industries. But an industry (a group of firms producing similar products or services) has fuzzy boundaries: similar according to which criteria? What if a firm belongs to several industries?
PESTEL scans the macro-environment: structural trends and uncertainties that shape an industry but that no single organization controls (although some have more power than others to shape them).

Porter's Five Forces explain the underlying profitability of an industry: where the economic value is located and which forces favour or impede capturing it. Growth alone does not make an industry attractive.
Political: government stability, taxation, social welfare policies, foreign trade regulation (e.g. return of US protectionism since 2025).
Economic: GDP, inflation, disposable income, interest rates, exchange rates (e.g. end of near-zero interest rates since 2022).
Social: shifts in values and culture, lifestyle, consumerism, attitudes to work and leisure (e.g. younger generations drinking less alcohol).
Technological: research policy, new patents and products (e.g. AI answers in search cut publishers' Google traffic).
Environmental: climate change, energy consumption, waste (e.g. shorter, less reliable snow seasons for ski resorts).
Legal: legislative and regulatory constraints and changes (e.g. EU board gender-balance quotas since June 2026).
How to use it – three steps:
children: Scan: identify the factors that matter for THIS industry, not generic ones like “inflation”
Assess: rate each factor on impact and predictability – trends you can plan on vs uncertainties that call for scenarios
Translate: ask for whom each factor is a threat or an opportunity

sections.heading: Porter's Five Forces – factors that increase each force

blocks.text: 1. Rivalry among existing competitors (same demand, similar products – not substitutes; e.g. Air France vs British Airways). Higher when:
children: Low concentration – power evenly distributed among rivals
Low industry growth → price competition
Low differentiation → price competition
High fixed costs → pressure for volume, price competition

blocks.text: 2. Threat of new entrants (how hard is it to enter? e.g. pharmaceuticals). The threat is LOW when entry barriers are high:
children: Scale and experience (economies of scale)
Access to supply or distribution channels
Incumbents' formal control: vertical integration, property rights (patents)
Incumbents' informal control: customer loyalty, networks, brand identity
Capital requirements (private tutoring vs private university)
Legislation (pharmaceuticals, pensions, taxis)

blocks.text: 3. Threat of substitutes: products with a similar function and benefit but a different nature (tablet vs computer, bus vs train, aluminium vs steel). They come from outside the industry – watch distant threats. Main driver: low switching costs (“cost” = value for money).
4. Bargaining power of buyers – the immediate customers, not necessarily final consumers (supermarkets buying milk). Higher when:
children: Buyers are concentrated
Switching costs are low / products standardized
Buyers can integrate backwards (produce in-house)

blocks.text: 5. Bargaining power of suppliers (oil & gas, Microsoft's operating system). Higher when:
children: Suppliers are concentrated
Switching costs for the buyer are high
Suppliers can integrate forwards
Suppliers' products are highly differentiated (strong brands vs milk producers)

blocks.text: The originality of the model: rivalry is not the only force. The four other forces put pressure on firms in the industry and all affect the first force.
Contributions:
children: Simplifies micro-economic theory, makes it applicable, encourages systems thinking
Shows that internal competition is not the only determinant of profitability
Helps predict long-term returns; profitability cannot be read from growth alone

blocks.text: Limitations:
children: Industry level rather than finer product-market segments
Forces treated as independent, while they are interdependent
Forces are not prioritized
Assumes rigid industry boundaries
Static view of today's forces

blocks.text: Rivalry high: saturated market (US households own 3 vacuums, 97 % of Japanese households own one), growth only in pockets such as China and cordless sticks.

Threat of entry high (low barriers); substitutes moderate (brooms, but no efficient alternative); suppliers' power high (oil prices drive plastics); buyers' power high (price-sensitive, well-informed).
Conclusion: an unattractive industry – yet Dyson earns high margins. The explanation lies in its differentiation and resources, not in industry structure (→ internal analysis, F5).
A group of firms producing products and services that are similar to each other.
A product with a similar function and benefit but of a different nature, coming from outside the industry.
The cost for a customer of moving from one offer to another (in value-for-money terms).
Obstacles that newcomers must overcome to enter an industry (scale, access, control, capital, legislation).
Buyers or suppliers taking over the activity of the other side (backward vs forward integration).

sections.heading: Further thinking: how to answer a Five Forces question

blocks.text: Go through all five forces, rate each (low / medium / high) and justify each rating with two or three facts from the case – the exam rewards reasoning, not lists.
Name the right buyers and suppliers: for an app, buyers can be users AND corporate clients; suppliers can be content creators, app stores (30 % fee) and cloud providers.
Conclude explicitly on attractiveness (“moderately attractive because …”) and mention one interdependence or one limitation (static view, blurred boundaries).
For PESTEL, pick only relevant factors, say whether each fosters or hinders the industry and for whom.
